sections.html:
• Scientific name: Mespilia globulus
  • Minimum tank size: 15 gallons (~60 liters)
  • Breeding: difficult
  • Salinity: SG 1.021–1.025
  • KH: 8–12
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: herbivorous / algae
  • Temperament: peaceful
  • Toxicity: no
  • Colour: velvety, dark blue or black bands between rows of short, brown or tan spines

The Tuxedo urchin is a species of echinoderm in the family Temnopleuridae (Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Echinodermata, Class Echinoidea, Order Camarodonta, Genus Mespilia). It is native to the tropical waters of the Indo-Pacific region, from Indonesia, the Philippines and southern Japan, throughout the Indian Ocean and the Western Atlantic Ocean.
It is generally found on shallow reef areas, seagrass beds and coral rubble, at depths of 0–60 m.

This species suits various tanks, including nano tanks of 40 litres, since it is small. Anything smaller causes feeding problems, as there may not be enough algae. Ideally use a tank of at least 60 litres or larger, especially if keeping more than one together with other animals, because they like to crawl and eat.

The Tuxedo urchin is a low-maintenance reef aquarium candidate and relatively easy to care for. It is safe to handle (not toxic).

Water conditions must be optimal and stable. Lighting intensity and water flow are best kept moderate; anything above that does more harm than good.

Carry out partial water changes (15% every two weeks or 25% monthly) to remove excess nitrate and replenish depleted trace elements.

The urchin is quite sensitive to poor water conditions, so maintain good water quality with routine maintenance (partial water changes, filter maintenance, etc.). Poor or varying parameters can make it lose its spines.

Acclimation

Acclimate it carefully, as with all invertebrates, very slowly (1–2 hours).

Common problems

Loss of spines: may be caused by nitrate above 10 ppm, acclimation shock, poor handling, high stress and poor water quality. Losing spines makes the urchin susceptible to microbial infections, which in most cases does not end well. Prevention: drip-acclimate slowly over a long period, matching the salinity to its previous environment, keep parameters stable, change water regularly and make sure it gets enough food.

Parasites: they eat the soft tissue of the urchin. If not removed, bald patches appear, get worse and the animal dies. Solution: manual removal; no chemical treatment is known to be safe for the urchin.

Scratches: urchins can leave etch marks on acrylic tanks. Solution: keep them in glass tanks.

• Temperature: 22–26 °C (tropical species)
  • Salinity: 1.021–1.025
  • Alkalinity: 8–11 dKH
  • pH: 8.1–8.4

The urchin has no special lighting requirements; lighting should be adapted to the needs of the Chaetomorpha and coralline algae in the tank.

Tuxedo urchins need many small items to be happy, since they cover themselves with things to disguise. Add empty shells, pebbles, rubble pieces, etc.; they drop them after a while when they no longer want to carry them. If they cannot find suitable items they get stressed. Being covered with things is a good sign of a healthy urchin.

Algae form a large part of the diet, so a mature aquarium with a steady supply of fresh filamentous algae is best. The urchin also eats debris and detritus, as well as macroalgae such as Chaetomorpha and coralline algae, which matters if you are trying to promote coralline growth. It may even eat Caulerpa when hungry. It eats nuisance algae such as hair algae, and filamentous microalgae and dried seaweed.

It should not be left with only this food. If there is not a plentiful supply of algae, supplement with dried seaweed sheets (nori), thin slices of carrot or spirulina. Keep supplemental food away from fish and other tankmates: spot feed by holding it right under the urchin until it climbs on top, or feed in the evening to reduce competition.

  • Diet type: omnivore
  • Preferences: algae
  • Feeding frequency: 1–2 times a week

The Tuxedo urchin is a peaceful, reef-compatible species and is unlikely to show aggression to other inhabitants despite its spines. It forages at night: during the day it is less active, lying on rocks or in crevices, and at night it comes out to scavenge or graze on algae. It eats a lot and produces a lot of waste. It is a heavy algae eater and is often seen cruising the glass and equipment, cleaning them.

It frequently picks up items lying around the tank (pebbles, algae, coral frags, snails, empty shells) and places them on itself to camouflage against predators. If it carries nothing, it may be sick or stressed.

  • Social: yes
  • Activity: low
  • Nocturnal: yes
  • Peaceful: yes
  • Burrowers: no

Reef safety: it does not eat corals and is safe for reef tanks. According to a study, urchins increased coral survivorship over 180 days and also increased coral growth rates, as microherbivory can play an important role. Tuxedos do not usually move or knock rockwork, but it is still recommended to glue corals to the rocks. They can even carry small, unattached zoanthids or other polyps without piercing them with their spines.

Tankmates: can be housed with various saltwater fish and invertebrates. Aggressive fish are not a big concern since the spines ward them off, but parrotfish and triggerfish sometimes eat them. Compatible examples: shrimp such as Sexy shrimp, Pederson cleaner shrimp, Red fire shrimp (Lysmata debelius), Peppermint shrimp (Lysmata wurdemanni) or Skunk cleaner (Lysmata amboinensis); snails such as Bumble bee snail, Fighting conch, Cerith snails, Trochus snails, Mexican turbo snails; also hermit crabs, clownfish, gobies, wrasses, zoanthids and mushrooms.
Sexes can only be told apart under a microscope; for example, the male genital papilla protrudes from the body surface, forming a short cone about 110 microns high.

The pet industry depends entirely on wild-caught animals, and there are only a few reports of successful breeding in a reef aquarium. If possible, choose captive-bred specimens, which are better adapted to aquarium life and more disease resistant.

  • Reproduces sexually; gonochoric, releasing gametes (sperm and eggs) into the water. Females can release up to 270,000 eggs.
  • Fully mature at a diameter of 2.0–2.5 cm.
  • Spawning occurs at both the full moon and the new moon, so the same individual may spawn twice a lunar month.
  • Fertilisation is external. Eggs float in the water.
  • Prismatic larvae start to feed on microalgae 3 days after fertilisation.
  • Embryos develop into planktotrophic larvae (echinoplutei) that live for many months in the water column; under optimal conditions metamorphosis occurs from 21 days after fertilisation.
  • They then sink to the bottom, attach with their tube feet and metamorphose into young urchins.
  • Juveniles have a mean diameter of around 1.53 mm 49 days after settlement.

Like most sea urchins, it is a spherical benthic animal with coloured bands and short (up to 6 mm) movable spines, which are flexible, used for locomotion and serve as passive defence; it is not poisonous. It is characterised by broad, velvety, dark blue or black bands between rows of short brown or tan spines. There is also a reddish variety (Mespilia cf. globulus) with blue or black bands and red spines. The skeleton, known as the 'test', is made of rigid, rounded calcareous plates, and the mouth faces downward near the substrate.

Fully grown, it measures roughly 7–8 cm in diameter; in aquariums the average size is near 5 cm.

There is no data on maximum lifespan in the wild. In captivity, life expectancy depends on water quality, living conditions and shipping stress. If well cared for, it can live up to 3 years, but the average is around 1–2 years.

About 1,000 sea urchin species are known worldwide; they belong to the same phylum as sea cucumbers, sand dollars, sea lilies, sea stars, sea biscuits and brittle stars.
